The first vocabulary list of the lesson. Every noun is given here with its article, which is the habit the book asks you to build: learn each noun together with o or a.
In Portuguese the word for wife is the same as the word for woman: mulher. There is also the more formal pair esposa (wife) and esposo (husband).
Two consonant pairs that appear constantly in Portuguese, and that you have already met in mulher and filha.

notes.title: The definite articles o and a

blocks.text: A noun refers to a person, place or thing. Very few English nouns have a masculine or feminine form — host/hostess is a rare one — but every noun in Portuguese has a grammatical gender. The definite article, the, is o for masculine and a for feminine, and it reflects that gender.
People
Places and things have a gender too
But the ending doesn't always tell you
o and a are used far more often than the is in English, and they always tell you the gender. So when you learn a new noun, learn it with its article — not casa but a casa.
One and two are the numbers that change with gender: they agree with the noun they refer to. You'll meet the rest of the numbers in the next lesson.

notes.title: Há — there is and there are

blocks.text: Há covers both there is and there are — one word, no change for number.
Negative
Put não (no) in front of há.
Questions

In writing, just add a question mark — there is no word inversion the way English flips to Is there? / Are there? Intonation does the work: a slight rise in pitch toward the end tells the listener it's a question.
Here and there

rows: Há um professor aqui e três estudantes ali.
There is a teacher here and three students there.
There's a good hotel over there.

notes.title: A minha família — bringing it together

blocks.text: The lesson closes with a short monologue in which a speaker introduces her family. Rather than reproduce it here, this is the pattern it drills — every sentence is há plus a family word plus a name, which is exactly what you'd say introducing your own.

rows: I want to introduce my family.
Na minha família há um pai, o Sr. Carlos.
In my family there's a father, Mr. Carlos.
Há uma mãe, a Sra. Ana.
There's a brother, Pedro, a teacher.
E há uma irmã, Sônia, médica.
And there's a sister, Sônia, a doctor.
Há dois avôs e duas avós.
There are two grandfathers and two grandmothers.
Há tios, tias, primos e primas.
There are aunts, uncles, and cousins.
Também há o Juca. O Juca é o cachorro!
There's also Juca. Juca is the dog!

blocks.text: Notice the definite article in front of names and family words — o Juca, a Sra. Ana, a minha família. Brazilians use it far more freely than English does. And note a person's job simply follows their name, with no article: Pedro, professor.

blocks.text: This one varies by region. In the south — Paraná, Santa Catarina, Rio Grande do Sul — people tend to pronounce t as it's spelled even before e or i. In Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo it becomes a ch.
Regional pronunciation doesn't drastically change the word — no more than an American and a British speaker saying their own t differently.
